analysis.one_liner: Offers federal grants to states, cities, and tribes that require licenses to buy a handgun.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee assignment; it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on January 26, 2023 and no vote was ever held before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill creates a competitive federal grant program to help states, local governments, and Indian tribes pay for handgun purchaser licensing programs. To qualify, a state must already have a law requiring a license to buy a handgun, with background checks, fingerprinting, an in-person application at a law enforcement agency, and renewal at least every five years. It does not mandate anything nationally — no state is required to adopt licensing; the federal money is simply an incentive for governments that choose to do it.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states, cities, and tribes that adopt or strengthen handgun licensing, who would get federal funding to run the programs. The bill's findings cite research associating handgun licensing laws with lower firearm homicide and suicide rates, including a Connecticut study showing a 27.8% reduction in firearm homicide rates after its 1995 law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states adopting handgun licensing

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes federal grants to States, local governments, and Indian tribes to develop, implement, and evaluate handgun purchaser licensing programs.

Grants are available only to applicants with a licensing law requiring applicants to be 21 or older, pass a background check, submit fingerprints and photographs, apply in person at a law enforcement agency, and renew at least every five years.

The bill's stated rationale cites research that adopting a licensing law in Connecticut was associated with a 27.8% drop in firearm homicide rates and a 32.8% drop in firearm suicide rates, while Missouri's repeal was associated with a 47.3% increase in firearm homicide rates.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the grants, with the authorization left open ('such sums as may be necessary'). Gun dealers and buyers in states that adopt licensing bear new steps — applications, fingerprints, fees, and waiting periods — though the federal government, not the states, foots the administrative bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers; handgun buyers in adopting states

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the funding level blank, authorizing 'such sums as may be necessary,' which gives no estimate of the cost to federal taxpayers.

Licensing requirements add steps — in-person applications, fingerprinting, and periodic renewal — that make handgun purchases slower and more expensive for buyers in participating states, a cost borne even by people who are law-abiding.

The program only affects states that voluntarily adopt licensing, so the research-based benefits the bill cites would apply unevenly, and state licensing laws vary in rigor — the grant conditions set minimums but allow states to define their own background-check standards beyond the federal floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is modest and voluntary: it adds no federal mandate and spends federal money only where states have already chosen to license handgun buyers. The main trade-off is that licensing adds time, fees, and paperwork to gun purchases in participating states, weighed against research the bill itself cites linking licensing to sizable reductions in gun homicides and suicides. The open-ended funding authorization is a fiscal blank check, but grant programs of this kind are typically small relative to overall federal spending.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it stayed; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Van Hollen introduced the bill on January 26, 2023, joined by Sens. Blumenthal and Murphy as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary — the only action ever taken on it.
The bill died in committee at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, with no further action recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Handgun retailers and buyers faced no new licensing incentives or requirements, and no federal grant spending was authorized. Residents of states considering licensing got no federal help to start programs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun retailers; no federal licensing funds were spent

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Handgun Permit to Purchase Act and led it through introduction.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no record of where members stood; the bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill does not regulate the industry directly, but in states that take the grants and adopt licensing, handgun sales become slower and more paperwork-heavy — and the research the bill cites associates licensing laws with lower firearm homicide rates, meaning fewer criminal-market sales. Retailers' interest in frictionless sales runs against the public-safety goal, though the voluntary design limits the impact outside adopting states.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies in participating states would receive federal money to run license applications, background checks, and fingerprinting — new administrative work at no cost to the state.
